mu.headline: Police investigate assault on 22-year-old guard at Roches-Noires charcoal factory
mu.dek: The guard was found critically injured at his workplace on 16 November after an apparent dispute over a motorcycle engine, police were told.
paragraphs: A 22-year-old security guard was found critically injured at a charcoal factory on Cremation Road in Roches-Noires on the night of Monday, 16 November. Police received an alert at about 23:45 and found him on a dirt path at the workplace.

The guard had serious injuries to his face and left foot, according to Ion News. Information gathered in the case indicated he had been hurt in an altercation with a man over a motorcycle engine. He was taken to SSRN Hospital in Pamplemousses and then treated by a SAMU medical team.

Police have opened an investigation. Defi Media reported that four young people were detained on 17 November in connection with the case; it said the injured guard, whom it described as 20, was receiving artificial breathing after surgery for blood clots.

mu.headline: Port-Louis waterfront festival returns with more than 30 food stalls
mu.dek: The 20-22 November event caps dish prices at Rs 275 and adds nightly concerts, DJ sets and radio activities.
paragraphs: The Port-Louis Waterfront Food Festival will return from 20 to 22 November for its second edition, with more than 30 food stalls offering Mauritian dishes and food inspired by Indian, Korean, other Asian and Western cuisines. The event is organised by Défi Digital and Radio Plus, with Pocket Island Solutions Ltd and Coca-Cola as partners.

Organisers say prices for dishes will not exceed Rs 275. The stalls will sell options including biryani, curries, noodles, dumplings, street food and seafood, alongside desserts and drinks. The festival follows a first edition held in July.

Concerts, DJ sets and other music performances are scheduled each evening from 19 to 21 hours. Radio Plus will also run games and activities, distribute gifts and bring its presenters to the waterfront during the three-day event.

mz.headline: Mozambique judge halts Mondlane trial over late 223-page defence filing
mz.dek: The Supreme Court hearing was paused about an hour early after the defence asked to distribute copies of its written response to other parties.
paragraphs: A judge halted the first session of politician Venâncio Mondlane’s trial at Mozambique’s Supreme Court on Tuesday, about an hour before its scheduled end, after his defence presented a 223-page written challenge. The lawyers asked to give copies to the other parties the following day.

Judge Luís Mondlane questioned why a document of that length had not been provided earlier, noting that the prosecution’s case had been filed months ago. The defence said it did not have copies available at the hearing. The judge said lawyers had a responsibility to submit such a filing in advance, then set the hearing to resume Wednesday at 10:00.

Before the pause, prosecutors read 107 points across 44 pages of charges. Mondlane faces five alleged crimes, including incitement to terrorism; prosecutors link his public calls for strikes and protests to violence and damage during the post-election period. The defence disputes the timing of a separate claim by road concessionaire Revimo, which alleges losses from damaged toll booths and unpaid road use.

mz.headline: Mozambique police urge calm as Mondlane’s Supreme Court trial opens
mz.dek: The former presidential candidate faces five charges linked to protests after the 2024 election, while his ANAMOLA party demands a fair and independent process.
paragraphs: Mozambique’s Supreme Court began the trial of Venâncio António Bila Mondlane, a former presidential candidate and leader of the ANAMOLA party, at 10 a.m. on Tuesday. He faces five charges following protests that began after the October 2024 election and continued until January 2025.

The Republic of Mozambique Police (PRM) called on citizens to remain calm and avoid actions that threaten public order or people and property, saying it would act preventively and proportionately. Police and armoured vehicles were deployed across Maputo, with water-cannon vehicles stationed at city access points and some peripheral neighbourhoods.

ANAMOLA said the trial must respect the presumption of innocence and Mondlane’s right to a defence, and be free of political pressure. The protests killed more than 350 people, mostly at the hands of police, according to the report; no police officer has been tried over those deaths.

na.headline: Namibia sets N$18 hourly minimum for security guards from January 2027
na.dek: The final stage of a three-year wage transition will lift the minimum from N$16 and cover more than 30 000 workers nationwide.
paragraphs: From 1 January 2027, more than 30 000 private security guards across Namibia will be paid no less than N$18 an hour, the last step in the sector's national minimum-wage transition. The floor climbed from N$13.50 in January 2025 to N$16 in January 2026.

Namibia Security Labour Forum (NSLF) said the rate applies to every type of security service, and that a 12-hour shift will bring at least N$216 before overtime, night-shift allowances and Sunday or public-holiday premiums. Employers may not take uniforms, boots, radios or patrol transport out of those minimum wages.

Government bodies, state-owned enterprises, businesses and households that buy security services were told to check their budgets and contracts before the change. The forum also wants regulations under the Security Enterprises and Security Officers Act brought in, arguing that tighter oversight would weed out non-compliant firms and raise training standards.

na.headline: Namibia's EU exports rise more than 17% to N$17.6 billion
na.dek: Exports to the bloc supported an estimated 40 000 direct jobs in 2025, a study presented in Windhoek found, with the EU now taking 19.4% of the country's total exports.
paragraphs: Namibia shipped more than N$17.6 billion of goods to the European Union in 2025, up over 17% from about N$15 billion a year earlier, an independent study presented at a Windhoek trade workshop on Monday found. That made the EU the country's third-largest export market, with 19.4% of total exports.

Working on the figures, EU Ambassador to Namibia Ana Beatriz Martins said the trade sustained an estimated 40 000 direct jobs across fisheries, farming, food processing and other productive sectors. The European market takes over half of Namibia's fish, fruit and vegetable exports and charcoal, and more than 80% of its meat exports.

The EU–Southern African Development Community Economic Partnership Agreement, which turns 10 this year, gives qualifying Namibian goods duty-free, quota-free entry into Europe. Martins said the bloc's new EPA Facility is meant to ease trade constraints and help small and medium-sized firms use the deal. Trade executive director Jerobeam Shaanika urged the country to move from raw materials to higher-value products.

na.headline: Namibia vehicle sales fall 6.2% to 1,188 in October
na.dek: Toyota registrations dropped by 106 from a year earlier, ending the market’s 18-month run of annual growth despite gains across other brands.
paragraphs: Namibia sold 1,188 new vehicles in October, down 6.2% from a year earlier and 20.7% from September’s 1,498, according to Simonis Storm Securities. The annual fall ended 18 consecutive months of growth. Sales in the first 10 months of 2026 were still up 10.6% to 13,453.

Toyota registrations fell to 637 from 743 a year earlier, a loss of 106 vehicles that exceeded the market’s total year-on-year decline of 79. All other brands combined rose 5.2% to 551, while Toyota’s market share dropped to 53.6% from 58.6%. Simonis Storm linked much of Toyota’s fall to weaker registrations of the Urban Cruiser, Starlet and Vitz, which together declined to 46 from 111.

Passenger vehicle registrations fell 10.6% to 490 and light commercial vehicles declined 2.7% to 619. Seasonally adjusted sales reached 1,179, their lowest level since February 2026; registrations outside Windhoek were down 2.3% in October, compared with an 8.2% fall in the capital.

na.headline: Telecom Namibia reports equipment thefts at northern sites
na.dek: The break-ins damaged infrastructure at sites in Oshakati, Ongwediva and Ondangwa, disrupting voice and data services, the company said.
paragraphs: Telecom Namibia recorded thefts and break-ins at telecommunication sites in Oshakati, Ongwediva and Ondangwa from 13 November and over the weekend, the company said. The incidents damaged infrastructure and equipment at several sites.

Spokesperson Ndapewa Nashila said in a statement released on Tuesday that affected locations included Oshakati Extension 16, Ekuku, Ehenye, Okaku and Efidi, as well as three sites at Evululuko and the Omashaka base station in Ondangwa. She said the disruption affects voice and data services used by emergency responders, businesses, schools, health facilities and residents.
Telecom Namibia urged residents to stay vigilant and report concerns, warning that similar sites could be targeted. The statement did not detail the value of stolen equipment or repairs.

na.headline: Gondwana shares begin trading on Namibia’s OTC market at N$9.60
na.dek: The tourism group’s shares are available through four stockbrokers, but its OTC quotation does not raise new capital and trades can be infrequent.
paragraphs: Gondwana Holdings shares began trading on the Namibia Securities Exchange’s Over-the-Counter Market on 13 November, allowing investors to buy or sell through four participating stockbrokers. The last recorded trade was on 19 October at N$9.60 a share.

ne.headline: Niger orders Mahamid Arabs to leave by 31 December
ne.dek: Several thousand members of the community, many settled in the south-east for decades, have been told to leave the country by the end of 2026.
paragraphs: Nigerien authorities have ordered the Mahamid Arab community to leave the country before the end of 2026, according to RFI Afrique. Local authorities announced that several thousand nomadic Mahamid Arabs living in south-east Niger must depart by 31 December.

Many Mahamid have lived in Niger for decades, and the first arrived from Chad and Sudan in the 1970s. Authorities have taken measures against the community for several months, and voices in the country have denounced serious discrimination.
The deadline applies to a community concentrated in the south-east, where it has lived for generations. Its members now have less than six weeks to decide whether and where to go.

ne.headline: Niger and Algeria advance technical work on trans-Saharan gas pipeline
ne.dek: An Algerian delegation is in Niamey from 17 to 20 November to settle route studies and operational steps for the Nigeria-to-Algeria project.
paragraphs: An Algerian delegation is in Niamey from 17 to 20 November 2026 to advance preparations for the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which would carry natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria. Niger’s petroleum ministry secretary-general, Abdoulkarim Mohamed Ali, received the delegation on 17 November on behalf of the petroleum minister.

The talks focused on speeding up technical studies of the pipeline’s route across Niger and setting the next operational steps needed to prepare for construction. The delegation includes officials from Algeria’s hydrocarbons ministry, SONATRACH’s pipeline transport branch and the National Pipeline Company.

Algeria has begun construction on its section, according to the Nigerien news agency. Niger’s project management unit, an interministerial committee and state petroleum-products company SONIDEP are also to support preparations; the government says the project is expected to raise public revenue, create jobs and develop local content.

ne.headline: Tiani appoints Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou to lead Niger’s national police
ne.dek: The former head of the country’s narcotics-trafficking office was named police director general by a decree signed on 13 November.
paragraphs: Niger’s President, Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani, appointed police commissioner general Aboubacar Issaka Oumarou as director general of the National Police in a decree signed on 13 November. Oumarou previously led the Central Office for the Suppression of Illicit Drug Trafficking.

Oumarou has held several senior police posts in Niger, including regional police director in Agadez and deputy director of public security. He also served in United Nations peacekeeping missions in Timor-Leste, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo, where he coordinated UN police in the east from Goma.

In Congo, he directed a project to train six rapid-intervention police battalions ahead of the 2011 general elections and led the UN police electoral group. The appointment puts him in charge of Niger’s national police as public security and citizen protection remain challenges, according to Agence Nigerienne de Presse.

ne.headline: Niger investment agency visits three firms receiving tax-code benefits

paragraphs: A delegation from Niger’s Agency for the Promotion of Private Investment and Strategic Projects (ANPIPS) visited three industrial firms in Niamey on 17 November to review operations, production capacity and their contribution to the economy. The firms—Murex SARLU, Nataro Agro SARL and Bénie SARLU—receive benefits under the investment code.

Murex produces A4 paper and employs 16 people, with capacity to make 800 cartons a day, equivalent to half a container of imported paper. Its director, Hachem Ibrahim Khalil, said the agency had advised and supported the factory. The company reported an investment of 641 894 848 FCFA and a tax exemption of 142 233 722 FCFA.

Nataro Agro, a natural-juice producer created by the Belvie group, reported an investment of 1 535 821 223 FCFA and an exemption of 417 166 514 FCFA. Company managers presented investments, production capacity and jobs during the visits; the report gave no figures for Bénie.

rw.headline: S&P keeps Rwanda's B+ rating as deficit forecast falls to 4.9% of GDP
rw.dek: The agency cites growth and concessional borrowing, and the airport's financing arrangement cut second-phase spending by Rwf168.2 billion in 2026.
paragraphs: Standard & Poor's (S&P) Global Ratings maintained Rwanda's B+ sovereign credit rating, citing economic growth, improved public financial management and the structure of external debt. The agency expects the fiscal deficit for the 2025/26 financial year to reach about 4.9% of gross domestic product, below the initially planned 5.7%, because tax revenues beat expectations and spending fell.

S&P said the economy grew 9.3% in 2025 and about 10% year on year in the first half of 2026, led by manufacturing and services. The Ministry of Finance reported public and publicly guaranteed debt of Rwf17.85 trillion by June, equal to 69.1% of GDP, down from 74.8% a year earlier. More than 87% of external debt consists of concessional loans, which carry lower interest rates and longer repayment periods.

The agency projects 7.5% growth in 2026 and an average of about 7% a year from 2027 to 2029. Financing involving the World Bank Group's International Development Association and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency reduced spending on the New Kigali International Airport's second phase by Rwf168.2 billion in 2026, and full commercial operations are expected around mid-2028.

st.headline: São Tomé swears in ADI leader Américo Ramos as prime minister
st.dek: President Carlos Vila Nova appointed Ramos after his party presented an agreement giving it support from 29 lawmakers, despite MLSTP objections.
paragraphs: Américo Ramos, leader of the Independent Democratic Action party (ADI), was sworn in again as prime minister of São Tomé and Príncipe on Monday, 16 November, at a ceremony led by President Carlos Vila Nova. ADI came second in the 27 September legislative election with 23 seats, behind the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe (MLSTP), which won 24.

Vila Nova’s decree said he appointed Ramos because ADI demonstrated parliamentary support through an agreement that gave it an absolute majority of 29 lawmakers. The MCI-PUN party grouping won six seats and BASTA won two. MLSTP contested the appointment and called on the president to reject any government led by ADI.

MLSTP lawmakers have also asked the Constitutional Court to annul the presidential decree. The party argued that the president failed to follow the constitutional rule requiring him to consider election results after consulting parliamentary parties; the presidency said MLSTP had not provided a written guarantee of governing support when consulted first.

st.headline: EMAE brings regular electricity to four communities in southern São Tomé
st.dek: Four low-voltage transformer stations now provide round-the-clock public-grid power in Yo Grande, Dona Augusta, Praia Pesqueira and Ribeira Peixe.
paragraphs: Four communities in southern São Tomé have gained regular electricity from the public grid for the first time, after the installation of four low-voltage transformer stations. The Empresa de Água e Eletricidade (EMAE), the country’s water and electricity company, supplies the network.

EMAE director-general Posik Espírito Santo said the communities now have power 24 hours a day. A consortium of oil companies funded the work; he credited Shell and Petrobras, through the National Petroleum Agency, with helping extend medium-voltage lines south to Porto Alegre. The new stations carry electricity into lower-lying areas.

Praia Pesqueira resident Ventura Vaz said homes previously relied on generators for about three to four hours a day. In Dona Augusta, José Luís Leal said children can now study and use the internet after school.

sn.headline: Faye meets Macron and investors on Paris leg of diplomatic tour
sn.dek: Senegal's president also held talks with Rothschild & Co and Vinci on energy, health and airport projects before the Francophonie summit in Cambodia.
paragraphs: President Bassirou Diomaye Faye completed a diplomatic tour of Paris and Phnom Penh on 16 November, after a trip from 9 to 16 November. In Paris on 9 November he met French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace, and the two discussed bilateral issues including preparations for an intergovernmental seminar and trade exchanges.

On 11 November Faye received leaders of industrial and financial groups, including Rothschild & Co and Vinci. Talks covered projects in energy, health and airport infrastructure, and how they would be financed. Faye presented Senegal's priorities and reforms aimed at improving investment security, according to Le Soleil.

The second leg took Faye to Phnom Penh on 15 and 16 November for the 20th Francophonie Summit, where discussions focused on choosing the next secretary-general of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), the organisation of French-speaking countries. Faye had also thanked France for its support for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

He is accused of promising a complainant that his wife would be hired as a director at the Port autonome de Dakar, with a monthly salary of 2.5 million CFA francs.

According to Libération, the alleged dealings began in March 2025. Fall allegedly collected 12,163,650 CFA francs as application fees, handed over a technician's diploma that was later found to be false, and promised a 15-day internship at a mining company in Ghana. He then allegedly demanded another 7 million CFA francs to unblock the file at the education ministry.

When the complainant checked, he reportedly found the diploma was false and no documents had been registered in his wife's name. He asked for his money back, but Fall allegedly refused and became unreachable. He has been arrested on suspicion of fraud and forgery; the allegations have not been proven.

sn.headline: Six teams qualify for 2027 Africa Cup of Nations
sn.dek: Mali, Burkina Faso, Benin, Cameroon and Morocco joined Senegal after Tuesday’s qualifying matches, with the final places still undecided.
paragraphs: Mali, Burkina Faso, Benin, Cameroon and Morocco qualified for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations on Tuesday, 17 November, joining Senegal as the first six teams confirmed for the tournament. The results came in the fourth round of qualifying matches.

Mali beat Rwanda 2-0 in Kigali, while Burkina Faso won 3-1 away to Mauritania. Burkina Faso’s victory also secured Benin’s place through its position in Group F; Mauritania and the Central African Republic are out of contention. Cameroon qualified without playing after Comoros beat Congo-Brazzaville 1-0, leaving Cameroon’s 10 points enough to guarantee a top-two finish in Group G.

Morocco secured qualification with a 1-0 win over Niger, its fourth consecutive victory. The remaining qualifying rounds will decide the other places in the 2027 tournament; Rwanda remains in contention for second in Group K.

sn.headline: Senegal arrests 26 in suspected irregular migration attempt at Abéné
sn.dek: The group included 24 Senegalese and two Gambians; investigators suspect two or three alleged organisers were posing as would-be migrants.
paragraphs: Senegalese gendarmes arrested 26 people on Abéné beach in the Kafountine area during the night of 16 to 17 November 2026, at about 4 a.m., after receiving information about a planned irregular migration departure. The group included 24 Senegalese and two Gambian nationals.

A security source said patrols intercepted two groups near the Kalisai hotel and Atlantique camp. The Senegalese group included two minors. Authorities took those arrested to the Kafountine brigade for identification and an investigation; initial findings suggest two or three suspected organisers were among them.

In the Kafountine-Diouloulou area, authorities have foiled 11 departures since the start of 2026 and arrested 183 would-be migrants and 13 alleged organisers or boat operators, according to Le Soleil. Seven departures were stopped by Kafountine’s local brigade and four by Diouloulou’s territorial brigade.

sn.headline: UCAD launches inclusion directorate and plans campus access work
sn.dek: The new office will assess community needs and oversee work on facilities for students with disabilities and psychological support.
paragraphs: Cheikh Anta Diop University of Dakar (UCAD) launched a Directorate of Inclusion, Well-being and Human Development on Tuesday, 17 November 2026. The office is built around inclusion and equity, cohesion and solidarity, well-being and mental health, and human development.

Its director, Amy Kébé Mané, said the office would first map university units and external partners working on inclusion and equality, then conduct a full assessment of the community’s needs. Three divisions will cover inclusion and changing practices, social action and solidarity, and well-being and psychological support for students and staff.

Mané said making the directorate operational was the immediate priority. Work is under way to refurbish a room for students with disabilities, renovate toilets and improve campus accessibility. The student association president said students were seeking rights, including access so no one is left behind.

sc.dek: Georges said the budget made no major announcements and was a small-change plan, cutting into the spending response the government had promised.
paragraphs: Bernard Georges, leader of the opposition in Seychelles' National Assembly, said the 2027 budget was a "small-change" plan that contained no major announcements. He made the comment on Wednesday morning while responding to Finance Minister Pierre Laporte's budget speech.

Laporte presented the budget speech on 22 November. Georges's criticism centred on the absence of major announcements, which he said made the proposal a minor adjustment rather than a shift in policy.
The report gives no spending totals or specific measures in the budget, and it does not say what the government will do next in response to the criticism.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone secures US$30 million under climate resilience programme
sl.dek: The Climate Investment Funds' ARISE programme announced the support at COP31 in Antalya, with financing arrangements and implementation still to be set out.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone secured US$30 million in climate investment support under the Climate Investment Funds' Accelerating Resilience Investments and Innovations for Sustainable Economies (ARISE) programme, announced on 12 November at the 31st Conference of the Parties in Antalya, Türkiye.

Environment and Climate Change Minister Jiwoh Emmanuel Abdulai said the recognition of Sierra Leone as a front-runner country under ARISE affirmed the government's commitment to resilience and adaptation. The announcement does not mean the funds have already entered government accounts; financing terms, project components, allocations and timelines will determine how they are deployed.

The government is expected to provide information on financing conditions, implementing institutions and intended beneficiaries. The article identifies coastal protection, urban drainage, climate-smart agriculture, water infrastructure, disaster preparedness and early-warning systems as possible priorities, with local communities involved in setting them.

sl.headline: Finance minister’s defender rejects call for his dismissal
sl.dek: Writer Foday M. Daboh says Sierra Leone’s economic hardship reflects global shocks, while arguing that Sheku Bangura restrained borrowing and inflation.
paragraphs: Foday M. Daboh has rejected a civil society consortium’s call to dismiss Sierra Leone Finance Minister Sheku Ahmed Fantamadi Bangura, arguing that economic hardship does not prove mismanagement. The consortium, identified as the CSOs Consortium on Public Accountability, demanded Bangura’s immediate removal.

Daboh says global disruptions between 2020 and 2024, including supply-chain problems, food and fuel inflation and tighter monetary policy, pressured economies. He argues Sierra Leone avoided default, retained access to concessional financing and stayed engaged with an International Monetary Fund programme under Bangura.

Citing Bank of Sierra Leone statements, Daboh says inflation later declined after fiscal and monetary tightening and reduced central-bank financing of deficits. He also acknowledges that Sierra Leone remains at high risk of debt distress, while saying borrowing is predominantly concessional and commercial borrowing has been restrained.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burners cut economic trees as demand grows
sl.dek: Environmental Protection Agency official Paul Lamin says the trade leaves land exposed and threatens food security, while 65-year-old Pa Alimamy depends on it for his family’s.
paragraphs: Charcoal production in Sierra Leone is cutting trees as households rely on the fuel for cooking, with 65-year-old burner Pa Alimamy saying the trade has kept him alive for more than two decades. He said his entire family depends on the work for income.

Paul Lamin, the Environmental Protection Agency’s director of natural resource governance, told Politico SL that burners now cut economic trees, including orange and mango, leaving land bare and threatening food security. Lamin said the trees take a long time to grow back, and acknowledged that people have few alternative energy sources.

The government’s National Energy Compact says 36% of the population has access to electricity and clean cooking reaches 15%. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates traditional wood energy produces 1/2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, or 2-7% of global human-caused greenhouse-gas emissions; sub-Saharan Africa accounts for one third of emissions from wood energy.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone passes 2027 MCC scorecard
sl.dek: The country met the benchmarks in an assessment of 104 nations, but passing does not guarantee it will receive development assistance.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone passed the Millennium Challenge Corporation’s 2027 Scorecard, meeting the required benchmarks in an annual assessment of national policy performance. The scorecard evaluates countries across 22 indicators covering governance, economic freedom and investment in people.

The corporation said 36 of the 104 countries assessed for fiscal year 2027 passed, while 68 failed to meet the benchmarks. The scorecards feed into a competitive process for development assistance, but the MCC board considers other factors when selecting countries, so Sierra Leone’s pass does not secure funding.
The MCC released the FY2027 country scorecards on Nov. 6, 2026. The assessment measures countries against the corporation’s policy standards.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone analysis says vice presidency offers no clear path to succession
sl.dek: Political economist Foday M. Daboh argues that the office has not helped any vice president win the presidency, citing Solomon Berewa’s 2007 defeat.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone political economist Foday M. Daboh argues that the vice presidency has not provided a clear route to the presidency, despite its constitutional position as the country’s second-highest office. In an analysis published in February 2026, he asks whether the pattern has already shaped the prospects of the current vice president.

Daboh says successive governments have used the office to balance regional, religious or ethnic interests, manage party factions and reward loyalty. He argues that vice presidents often enter without an independent political base or a defined succession path.

He points to Solomon Ekuma Berewa, who became the Sierra Leone People’s Party candidate for president in 2007 but lost to Ernest Bai Koroma. Daboh also cites former vice president Samuel Sam-Sumana, who was expelled from his party after becoming estranged from the president.

so.headline: World Bank weighs suspending Somalia budget support after court ruling
so.dek: The bank is considering a temporary funding halt after the Supreme Court said President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term ended on May 15, 2026.
paragraphs: Africa Intelligence reported on Monday that the World Bank is considering a short pause in budget support to Somalia, following a Supreme Court ruling that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term has run out. The court said his four-year term ended on May 15, 2026, and that the mandates of both houses of parliament ended on April 14.

Issued on Nov. 5, the ruling gave political leaders 30 days to agree on an electoral framework and 90 days to hold elections, while restricting the government to routine caretaker duties. The court held that constitutional amendments extending terms from four years to five did not apply retrospectively. The presidency has disputed parts of the court's jurisdiction and findings.

Budget support has recently been projected at $150 million or more a year, with the World Bank a major provider. Somalia's 2026 budget framework projected about $1.3 billion in revenue and grants, including nearly $470 million in domestic revenue. A pause would hit the federal government's ability to meet recurrent costs, including salaries and transfers to federal member states.

so.headline: Mohamud accuses UAE of seeking to divide Somalia and Sudan
so.dek: The Somali president said the Emirates had returned from Libya and Yemen divided, as Somalia faces disputes over elections and regional authority.
paragraphs: Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the United Arab Emirates of seeking to divide Somalia and Sudan in a video message released by his office on Tuesday. He said the Emirates had returned from Libya and Yemen divided, and urged people dealing with it to study those experiences.

The remarks came weeks after Somalia’s Constitutional Court ruled that parliament’s extension of Mohamud’s term was unlawful and ordered elections within 90 days. The government rejected the ruling and occupied the court’s premises; the chief justice and five other judges then sought shelter at former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed’s residence in Mogadishu after receiving death threats, according to Somali Guardian.

Mohamud’s government is also in dispute with opposition leaders, while relations with Puntland and Jubaland have deteriorated into intermittent military clashes. The report says there is no agreed election path; in the Southwest, forces loyal to ousted regional leader Abdiasis Laftagaren reclaimed five towns in Bay last month.

so.headline: Somaliland detains five Americans over alleged national security threat
so.dek: The intelligence agency said it monitored the US nationals after their arrival; a person familiar with the matter said they left on Monday.
paragraphs: Somaliland’s National Intelligence Agency said it briefly detained five US nationals over what it described as a threat to national security. In a post on X late Sunday, the agency said it had monitored them since they arrived and investigated their activities.

A person familiar with the matter said the five worked for Parallel Black, a US company, and left Somaliland on an Ethiopian Airlines flight on Monday afternoon. A November 4 letter seen by Reuters showed Somaliland’s foreign affairs minister had invited them to conduct feasibility studies for potential investments.

The agency’s director-general, Jama Mohamoud Egal, Somaliland’s foreign affairs ministry and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Parallel Black also did not immediately respond.

ss.headline: South Sudan Supreme Court directs Ajing to seek release from prosecutor
ss.dek: The court said it cannot order temporary release while the former presidential office director’s criminal case remains under investigation.
paragraphs: South Sudan’s Supreme Court on Tuesday, November 17, declined to grant temporary release to Ajing Deng Ajing, a former Executive Director in the Office of the President, while his criminal case remains under investigation. The Constitutional Panel directed him to apply to the Office of the Public Prosecutor.

The judges said Ajing faces charges in Criminal Case No. 710 of 2026. His lawyers alleged that his detention violated his rights and that he lacked access to legal counsel, family members and medical care; the respondents argued the detention was lawful and release requests must follow criminal procedures.

The ruling addresses only temporary release, not the legality of his arrest or detention. Ajing’s constitutional petition against the National Security Service and the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs remains pending, with proceedings scheduled to resume on December 15, 2026.

ss.headline: Jonglei plans to move 135 Akobo exam candidates to Bor
ss.dek: The state says it will cover food and accommodation, but opposition officials and parents are still deciding whether to accept the plan.
paragraphs: Jonglei State is consulting opposition officials and parents about moving 135 candidates from Akobo County to Bor after insecurity stopped them sitting national primary and secondary examinations in Akobo. The candidates are registered for both levels.

Moses Majok Gatluak, Jonglei’s caretaker governor, told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday evening that the state would pay for their transport, food and accommodation. He said the National Examinations Council had cancelled exams in the opposition-controlled area over security concerns, and that the national examinations ministry would make separate arrangements for candidates who had missed the start.

John Wiyual Lul, the opposition-appointed Akobo commissioner, said officials would meet candidates and parents on Wednesday to discuss relocation and decide whether to go to Bor. Primary examinations began on November 16; secondary exams are scheduled to start on November 23.

sd.headline: White Nile sets diesel at SDG 69,842.50 a gallon as farmers report shortages
sd.dek: The state also priced petrol at SDG 53,365 a gallon, while farmers say scarce diesel is disrupting irrigation in Um Rimta.
paragraphs: Authorities in Sudan’s White Nile State raised diesel and petrol prices on Monday, setting diesel at SDG 69,842.50 a gallon and petrol at SDG 53,365 in Kosti, Rabak, Al-Qitaina and Al-Duweim. The increases drew criticism from residents and farmers.

Hammad Musa, a farmer in Um Rimta, said a fuel container cost between SDG 600,000 and 800,000 and that farmers in the Al-Bugha agricultural schemes needed more diesel after three rounds of irrigation. He warned that shortages threatened their harvests and accused unidentified parties of diverting fuel to the black market. Gismallah Al-Tayyib, another farmer, alleged that fuel was being sold from filling stations on the black market with security forces involved.

The state’s Public Transport Regulation and Development Council also set a transport surcharge of SDG 20 per gallon of commercially priced fuel in Um Rimta, Tendelti, Rural Al-Duweim and Al-Jabalain, and SDG 100 per gallon in Al-Salam. Farmers called on authorities to prioritise fuel supplies for agriculture.

sd.headline: Drone strikes drive most civilian deaths in Sudan, UN rights office finds
sd.dek: The UN Human Rights Office counted more than 2,230 civilians killed in Sudan from January to October, with over 1,630 of those deaths caused by drones.
paragraphs: Drone strikes accounted for more than 80 per cent of the 1,390 civilian deaths recorded in Sudan between January and June 2026, a UN Human Rights Office report published on Wednesday shows. The fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces and allied armed movements has been documented across the country, with the office describing drone attacks as a defining feature of the war.

Another 840 civilians were killed in the following four months, close to 520 of them in drone strikes. The office said the figures it could confirm are likely lower than the true toll. Kordofan bore more than two-thirds of documented casualties, and Darfur most of the rest, while White Nile recorded at least 41 civilian deaths.

Over the first half of 2026, the office recorded at least 39 drone strikes on markets, 20 on civilian vehicles, 17 on fuel tankers and depots, and 16 on health facilities. High Commissioner Volker Türk said the findings describe serious violations of international humanitarian law that may amount to war crimes.

sd.headline: GERD operations leave Sudan’s Roseires dam exposed to sudden flow changes
sd.dek: A study says releases from Ethiopia’s newly opened dam can alter levels at Sudan’s irrigation hub within hours, affecting water supplies and farms.
paragraphs: A study published in Water International says operational decisions at Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam increasingly shape Sudan’s water security, with changes in releases affecting levels at Roseires Dam within hours. The study was written by water experts Yasser Abbas Mohamed, Azza Mustafa and Saif El-Din Hamad Abdullah.

The researchers cite a 2020 first filling without prior notice that lowered Blue Nile levels and temporarily disrupted Khartoum’s water purification plants. They also say unannounced releases in September 2025 contributed to flooding in agricultural and residential areas north of Roseires.

Negotiations between Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt have lasted more than 15 years without producing a legally binding operating agreement. The researchers say regulated flows could reduce severe seasonal floods and improve hydroelectric efficiency, but that cooperation is needed to achieve those benefits.

sd.headline: Amnesty urges war-crimes inquiry into RSF drone strikes in El Obeid
sd.dek: The rights group says nine attacks killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026, hitting homes and civilian infrastructure.
paragraphs: Amnesty International called for an investigation into Rapid Support Forces drone strikes in El Obeid, the capital of Sudan’s North Kordofan State, as possible war crimes. The group said it examined nine strikes in the city and its surroundings between June and August 2026, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10.

Amnesty said three strikes hit residential areas, four hit civilian infrastructure including the power plant, fuel stations and main market, and two targeted moving vehicles. The group said it found no military objectives near the strike sites at the time. It based its findings on interviews with 29 people from El Obeid, conducted between July and September 2026.

Amnesty Secretary General Agnès Callamard urged the United Nations and African Union to propose and implement civilian protection measures, including a protection force in Sudan. She also called for the United Nations Security Council to extend the arms embargo covering Darfur to the rest of Sudan and include drones.

tg.headline: Houngbo wins second five-year term leading UN labour agency
tg.dek: The Togolese former prime minister secured 51 of 56 votes after Spain’s labour minister withdrew as his only challenger.
paragraphs: Gilbert Houngbo of Togo was re-elected on 16 November to lead the International Labour Organization, the United Nations agency for labour issues, for a second five-year term. He received 51 of 56 votes cast.
Spain’s Labour Minister Yolanda Díaz Pérez withdrew her candidacy shortly before the vote, leaving Houngbo as the sole candidate. His new term is due to begin on 1 October 2027.

Houngbo said he would put artificial intelligence among the agency’s central challenges and argued that technological progress should serve people. Díaz Pérez said she withdrew after union leaders backed Houngbo, and criticised the agency’s financial position.

tn.headline: Tunisia launches €60 million green finance programme for small businesses
tn.dek: The facility will channel an initial €40 million through local banks, with EU grants paid to firms after their projects are verified.
paragraphs: Tunisia launched the Green Economy Financing Facility in Tunis on 16 November 2026, with about €60 million to help small and medium-sized businesses invest in energy and environmental improvements. The programme is a partnership between the European Union, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Tunisian authorities, and was announced by the EU ambassador to Tunisia, Giuseppe Perrone.

In its first phase, €40 million in credit lines will go to Tunisian banks, which will finance the investments of eligible firms. Amen Bank and the Union Bancaire pour le Commerce et l'Industrie (UBCI) each have an initial €10 million line, and a second €10 million agreement with UBCI was signed at the launch. Attijari Bank has signed a memorandum of understanding for a similar operation. Grants of 10 to 15% of eligible investment value are paid to firms after the EU verifies that projects have been completed.

The programme focuses on energy efficiency, renewable energy, sustainable construction and the circular economy, with water management and climate adaptation projects also included. Over time it will be extended to leasing companies and microfinance institutions.

tn.headline: Tunisia advances Grand Tunis mobility plan toward 2040
tn.dek: The study covers four governorates and will assess transport scenarios before officials select a plan for the region.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s equipment and housing minister, Salah Zouari, reviewed progress on a strategic urban mobility study for Grand Tunis on Tuesday, 17 November. The plan, being developed with support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), is intended to guide transport and urban planning in the region through 2040.

The study, led by the Grand Tunis Urban Planning Agency, covers Tunis, Ariana, Ben Arous and Manouba. A household travel survey conducted from January to March 2026 gathered information from a sample of 7000 households across the four governorates to map current travel patterns and inform future planning scenarios.

Officials are to complete and evaluate the proposed scenarios before choosing one for Grand Tunis. The reference plan is intended to guide public policy and planned investment, while addressing congestion, pollution, travel safety and sustainability.

tn.headline: Tunisia advances North African drug-regulation coordination in Cairo
tn.dek: At the committee’s second meeting, Tunisia and regional partners reviewed work on inspections and agreed on strategic documents for harmonising medicine procedures.
paragraphs: Tunisia took part on 17 and 18 November in Cairo in the second meeting of a North African initiative to coordinate medicine regulation. The gathering reviewed progress and work by groups covering inspections, pharmacovigilance, quality management and information systems.

The National Medicines and Health Products Agency (ANMPS), which represents Tunisia in the initiative, said the country holds its secretariat. Its director general, Soumaya Miled, represented Tunisia. Participants approved several strategic documents and examined ways to unify procedures for evaluating and registering medicines.

The initiative seeks to improve access to safe, effective and quality medicines while strengthening health security and pharmaceutical sovereignty across North Africa. Its inaugural meeting was held in Cairo from 18 to 20 February 2025, when the steering committee’s bureau was formed and initial strategic directions set.

tn.headline: Tunis court sentences Leïla Trabelsi’s sister to 21 years
tn.dek: The financial-corruption chamber also imposed heavy fines in a case involving corruption and the appropriation of public funds.
paragraphs: A specialised financial-corruption chamber at Tunis’s Court of First Instance sentenced a sister of Leïla Trabelsi, wife of former president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, to 21 years in prison on Monday, 16 November 2026. The case concerned financial and administrative corruption and the appropriation of public funds, Webdo reported, citing Mosaique FM.

The woman was tried while at liberty and did not attend Monday’s hearing. Her lawyer sought a postponement, citing health reasons that prevented her from appearing, but the chamber deliberated and issued its ruling. The court also imposed heavy financial fines; the report did not give their amount.

The same chamber sentenced her to four years in January 2026 in a money-laundering and foreign-exchange case. In a separate case over a public contract won by a company run by the woman and her husband, she, her husband and two foreign nationals received six-year terms and fines exceeding 20 million dinars. The four defendants appealed that ruling.

tn.headline: Tunis hosts six-day Italian-Tunisian arts festival in the medina
tn.dek: The programme runs through 21 November across cultural venues and schools, with most events free to attend.
paragraphs: The second Mediterraneo in movimento festival opened on 16 November at the Sainte-Croix cultural complex in Tunis’s medina, with events also taking place at other cultural venues and educational institutions in the capital. The six-day programme brings together art, music, cinema, theatre, photography and creative workshops focused on Italy and Tunisia.

Organised by Italian association Tararì Tararera Aps and partners in Bentivoglio and Cento, the festival includes an exhibition pairing Tunisian artist Aymen Mbarki with Italian artist Marco Pellizzola. A photography show by Tunisian photographer Nizar Rejeb presents 32 black-and-white images of Rome. Most events are free, and the first edition drew more than 500 people.

Italian director Pietro Marcello is due to lead a masterclass at the Higher Institute of Multimedia Arts on 20 November, followed by a screening of his film Martin Eden at the Tunisian Cinematheque. The festival closes on 21 November with a performance by the Coro delle Mondine of Bentivoglio, a concert by Tunisian musician Ragheb Ouergli and a public gathering.

eh.headline: Morocco jails four Sahrawi students for two years over peaceful protest
eh.dek: A Rabat court also fined each student 15,000 dirhams, about 1,400 euros, for joining a demonstration outside the prison administration in October.
paragraphs: The Rabat court of first instance on Friday sentenced four Sahrawi students, Brahim Babeit, Salah Eddine Essabar, El Hussein Chihab and Mohamed Lmrabet, to two years in prison and a fine of 15,000 dirhams each, about 1,400 euros. Their offence was joining a gathering on 12 October outside the Moroccan prison administration's headquarters in Rabat, to call for the release of Gdeim Izik prisoners on hunger strike.

Three others detained alongside them, human rights defenders, had their complaints dismissed and were freed within days. The four students were sent to Salé prison and held until sentencing. Two Spanish jurists who travelled to Rabat to follow the trial, representing the International Association of Lawyers for Western Sahara and the Spanish bar, were prevented from entering the courtroom.

Babeit refused to give a statement to the prosecutor until he received care and ended up in hospital. Sahrawi rights groups CODESA and CODAPSO said he was beaten during his arrest, and the prosecutor ordered a medical examination. Those medical records were among documents missing from the file, which had caused the trial to be postponed in October. He was convicted regardless.

eh.headline: EUCOCO closes in Madrid after speakers challenge diplomacy over Western Sahara
eh.dek: The 50th European conference ended with calls for another path as the United Nations mission in the territory entered liquidation on 1 November.
paragraphs: The 50th European Conference of Coordination of Support and Solidarity with the Sahrawi People (EUCOCO) met in Madrid on 13 and 14 November, ending with speakers saying diplomacy had failed and another path was needed. The gathering coincided with the 51st anniversary of the Madrid Accords.

Mansur Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative to Europe and European institutions, said the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara had not protected Sahrawis and described it as a “silent witness”. The mission has been in liquidation since 1 November, after the Security Council failed to approve either of two draft resolutions put to a vote on 30 October.

Sidi Mohamed Dadda, a former Sahrawi prisoner and activist in the occupied territories, warned that the mission’s end was dangerous, saying it had never had a human-rights mechanism. He cited four Sahrawi students sentenced in Rabat on 13 November to two years in prison and a fine of 15,000 dirhams each. Spain was due to vote on 29 November.

ls.headline: Western Cape water allocations cut as dam storage drops
ls.dek: Water and Sanitation Minister Pemmy Majodina announced a 7% cut for domestic and industrial users and 15% for irrigation.
paragraphs: Water allocations in South Africa's Western Cape are being reduced because dam storage has fallen under the preferred operating benchmark set by the Department of Water and Sanitation. Majodina announced a 7% reduction for domestic and industrial users and a 15% reduction for irrigation on Monday, measures expected to save 56.8 million cubic metres a year.

The Western Cape Water Supply System, which serves Cape Town, the West Coast and agricultural users, held 72.5% of capacity on November 2, or 646.5 million cubic metres, against a benchmark of 80%. A year earlier it stood at 84.4%. Below-normal winter rainfall has cut storage, and a forecast strong to extreme El Niño could mean hotter weather, more evaporation and less runoff.

Majodina urged municipalities, businesses, farmers and households to save water and keep clear of their full allocations. The department says the system remains stable and can meet current needs, but it will keep tracking dam levels, climate and demand, and may take further steps if conditions worsen.

paragraphs: ’Malerato Khutlisi, a councillor for the Revolution for Prosperity (RFP) party, has been elected the new Mayor of Maseru. paragraphs: Mathaleha Molapo won the Maseru Golf Club Corporate League November tournament on Friday, scoring 39 points. She tied with Mphaphathi Moshoeshoe, who also scored 39 points, but Molapo won on countback due to her lower handicap of 22. Setšabe Lefosa came in third place with 37 points.

The tournament was sponsored by Momentum Health Lesotho, which recently transitioned from Metropolitan Health Lesotho. Momentum Health Lesotho Finance Manager Semethe Lephosa stated the event was a success and pledged future sponsorships. He noted the tournament provided an opportunity to showcase the company's new identity.

Momentum Health Lesotho offers healthcare and insurance solutions in Lesotho and South Africa. Lephosa encouraged the public to obtain insurance for life protection. The Maseru Golf Club Corporate League holds monthly tournaments sponsored by various corporations.
